enrichment.short_title: Attorney General obtains indefinite civil proceedings order against Dr Saxena for habitual vexatious litigation
key_facts: The Attorney General applied under section 42 of the Supreme Court Act 1981 for a civil proceedings order against Dr Ram Pratap Saxena, prohibiting him from instituting or continuing civil proceedings without High Court leave.

Multiple judges had previously dismissed his applications as hopeless, misconceived or an abuse of process; Grepe v Loam orders had also been made against him.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Ex parte application by the Attorney General (following referral from Scott-Baker J) for a civil proceedings order; heard by the Administrative Court after personal service on the respondent.
enrichment.outcome: Civil proceedings order made without limit of time; Dr Saxena may not commence or continue civil proceedings without leave of the High Court.
enrichment.ratio: Where a person has habitually and persistently and without reasonable grounds instituted civil proceedings, and has been given a fair opportunity to be heard, the court may and in an appropriate case should make a section 42 civil proceedings order; given the history and duration of the conduct, an order without time limit may be justified.
legal_issues: Whether Dr Saxena had habitually and persistently instituted civil proceedings without reasonable grounds
Whether he had been given a proper opportunity to be heard
Whether the civil proceedings order should be for a specified period or without limit of time

enrichment.short_title: Party wall Kango hammer damage: adjoining owner entitled to robust causation inference where no section 3 notice served
key_facts: Roadrunner Properties owned 14 Molasses Row; adjoining owner Mr Dean had party wall work done at number 16 using a Kango 950 hammer drill to cut a chase for radiator pipes without serving a section 3 notice.

Floor tiles in Roadrunner's conservatory buckled and plaster cracked shortly after the works; the county court judge preferred the defendants' expert theory of moisture expansion over coincidence with the hammer work.
The claim grew from about £6,700 to over £16,000 after amended pleadings; competing single and separate experts were instructed after procedural changes.
Defendants had orally offered to relay tiles shortly after the complaint but the claimant refused.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from Mayor's and City of London County Court (HHJ Cox) on liability and quantum for party wall damage; further submissions on damages and costs after allowing appeal in part.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed in part on causation for conservatory floor tiles and wall cracks; damages fixed at £1,740; claimant awarded costs below and on appeal despite recovering a small fraction of the claim.
enrichment.ratio: Where a building owner carries out party wall works without the statutory notice and dispute-resolution procedure, a court should take a robust approach to causation: if damage is of a kind reasonably expected from the works, hypothetical post hoc expert explanations should be treated sceptically; temporal coincidence with percussive work on the party wall is a legitimate forensic factor.
legal_issues: Whether damage to the conservatory floor and walls was caused by the party wall works
Whether failure to serve a Party Wall Act notice affected the evidential burden on causation
Whether the trial judge erred in preferring the defendants' expert evidence
Appropriate use of single joint experts under CPR rule 35.7

enrichment.short_title: London reinsurers retain jurisdiction to pursue avoidance claim despite Spanish insurance dispute and failed jurisdiction clause argument
key_facts: London market reinsurers sought declarations avoiding or limiting liability under 2000/01 personal accident reinsurance of Real Sociedad football players, following Musini's underlying insurance claim for player Frederic Peiremans.
Musini applied to set aside English proceedings, arguing a Spanish jurisdiction clause in the underlying insurance was incorporated into the reinsurance slip via a full reinsurance clause.
Real Sociedad had commenced earlier proceedings in San Sebastian; Musini also relied on Article 28 related actions.
During the hearing the reinsurers undertook not to pursue the pre-existing condition alternative claim, narrowing the Article 28 dispute.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application by Musini in the Commercial Court for declaration of no jurisdiction, dismissal or stay under Articles 23 and 28 of Regulation 44/2001.
enrichment.outcome: Musini's application dismissed on the reinsurers' undertaking to confine the claim to avoidance; English court retains jurisdiction.
enrichment.ratio: A jurisdiction clause in underlying Spanish insurance is not clearly and precisely incorporated into a London reinsurance slip through a general full reinsurance clause, especially where ancillary terms such as jurisdiction are not expressly referenced; Article 28 does not require dismissal or stay where the avoidance claim focuses on non-disclosure of documents rather than the player's medical condition litigated in Spain.
legal_issues: Whether Article 23 jurisdiction agreement conferred exclusive jurisdiction on Spanish courts
Incorporation of jurisdiction clauses through full reinsurance and follow-the-settlements wording
Whether English and Spanish proceedings were related actions under Article 28
Whether the court should exercise discretion to dismiss or stay under Article 28

enrichment.short_title: Magistrates need not recite burden of proof in reasons when rejecting self-defence in nightclub assault conviction
key_facts: Pearson was convicted of common assault at Leeds Magistrates' Court after punching Stephen Tatterton on a nightclub dance floor in December 2001.
Pearson claimed he struck in self-defence after being hit first; he had attended the club to see his ex-girlfriend and was emotional, whereas Tatterton appeared calm.

Magistrates found Tatterton credible, rejected partial prosecution witness evidence on the fight itself but accepted evidence of his relaxed demeanour, and concluded Pearson had sought to attack Tatterton.
Pearson lost his job as a legal executive following the conviction; no costs order was made on appeal.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal by way of case stated to the Divisional Court (Lord Chief Justice and Mackay J) against magistrates' conviction and adequacy of reasons.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; magistrates were entitled to convict and their reasons were sufficient despite not expressly referencing burden and standard of proof.
enrichment.ratio: Magistrates need not express reasons in elaborate form or expressly recite the criminal standard of proof; comparing conflicting accounts is not necessarily a balance-of-probabilities approach where reasons identify specific credibility findings and conclude the act was aggression not self-defence; partial rejection of a witness's evidence on one issue does not require rejection of all their evidence.
legal_issues: Whether magistrates' reasons implied the wrong standard of proof when comparing accounts
Whether rejection of inconsistent prosecution witness evidence invalidated the conviction
Whether magistrates failed to find the prosecution had disproved self-defence

enrichment.short_title: Local ombudsman had no jurisdiction to investigate home student status complaint after claimant had pursued judicial review
key_facts: Claimant Scholarstica Umo, a Nigerian pharmacy student at De Montfort University, was wrongly told by Enfield LBC in 2000 that she qualified for home student status and student loan funding.

Enfield had offered £500 compensation; the university consent gave her roughly £25,000 benefit over four years.

enrichment.outcome: Claim for judicial review refused; commissioner lacked jurisdiction under section 26(6)(c) and proviso did not apply after resort to court.

Whether the commissioner should have exercised discretion under the proviso
Whether the April 2000 decision was distinct from matters already litigated

enrichment.short_title: Unsafe convictions where late similar-fact direction on cross-corroboration was garbled and omitted innocent contamination guidance
key_facts: Appellant was convicted on multiple counts of sexual offences against his daughter S (1987–1992) and niece D (1972–1975), separated by over a decade.
Prosecution opened that each complainant's evidence should be considered separately; only after all evidence did the Crown seek a mutual corroboration direction, which the judge granted.
Defence argued surprise and unfairness; some cross-examination on collusion occurred but not detailed comparison of similarities.
Judge's summing-up on similar fact was unclear on collusion, used 'will be satisfied' rather than 'may be satisfied', and lacked proper innocent contamination direction.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against conviction following trial at Kingston Crown Court (HHJ Hucker); single judge granted leave on late similar-fact direction ground; retrial application deferred.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed on defective summing-up alone; convictions quashed as unsafe; bail refused pending Crown decision on retrial.
enrichment.ratio: Although late introduction of cross-corroboration directions did not here render the trial unfair like R v Davies and Poolton, where the judge gives such directions he must do so with crystalline clarity including proper collusion and innocent contamination guidance per JSB specimen directions; garbled directions on similar fact can make convictions unsafe.
legal_issues: Whether the defence was unfairly surprised by the similar-fact direction after trial conduct on a separate-evidence basis
Whether counts relating to S and D were properly joined and tried together
Whether the judge's directions on cross-corroboration were adequate

enrichment.short_title: IAT rationally refused leave to appeal where asylum grounds misapplied Arif on burden of proof

statutes_considered.title: Immigration and Asylum Appeals Procedure Rules 2000

key_facts: Guinean national Mr Traore claimed asylum based on mistaken identity detention, torture and escape in February 2001.
The adjudicator largely accepted his account of ill-treatment in Guinea but rejected his journey to the UK and found no continuing Refugee Convention or ECHR risk on return.
Leave to appeal to the IAT focused on a misapplied burden-of-proof argument based on Arif and country conditions.
The IAT refused leave, holding the adjudicator could find no risk on return despite accepting credibility on past events.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of Immigration Appeal Tribunal decision refusing leave to appeal against adjudicator's dismissal of asylum appeal.
enrichment.outcome: Application for judicial review refused; IAT decision not irrational and disclosed no error of law.
enrichment.ratio: On an application for leave to appeal under rule 18, the tribunal is not required to consider grounds beyond those in the application; supervisory review requires a readily discernible obvious point in the claimant's favour not taken in the grounds—persuasive arguments developed at judicial review that were not before the IAT do not suffice.
legal_issues: Whether the IAT irrationally refused leave to appeal
Whether the adjudicator's reasoning from accepted torture to no future risk was flawed
Scope of judicial review where new arguments were not raised before the IAT

enrichment.short_title: Non-EC subsidiaries cannot recover ACT via double taxation non-discrimination articles or Article 56 where Article 57 preserves pre-1994 restrictions
key_facts: UK subsidiaries of Japanese (NEC) and US (Bush Boake Allen) parents paid advance corporation tax on dividends to non-UK resident parents because group income elections under section 247 were unavailable.
Claimants sought restitution relying on OECD-model non-discrimination articles in UK double taxation agreements with Japan, USA and Switzerland.

Park J held the articles would prohibit discrimination in principle but section 788(3)(a) did not incorporate relief from ACT into domestic law because ACT is not corporation tax in respect of income or chargeable gains.
Alternative Article 56 capital movement argument failed because Article 57(1) preserved pre-1994 restrictions on capital movements involving direct investment from third countries.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Group litigation order test case in Chancery Division following Metallgesellschaft/Hoechst; claim for restitution of ACT and interest.
enrichment.outcome: Claims dismissed; no reference to CJEC on Article 56; non-discrimination and EC Treaty grounds both rejected.
enrichment.ratio: Double taxation agreement non-discrimination provisions are not self-executing: only effects falling within section 788(3)(a)–(d) become part of UK tax law, and relief from ACT is not relief from corporation tax in respect of income or chargeable gains; Article 57(1) excludes from Article 56 prohibitions national restrictions on capital movements to third countries involving direct investment existing on 31 December 1993, covering ACT on dividends to non-EC parents.
legal_issues: Whether non-discrimination articles in double taxation treaties entitled non-EC subsidiaries to group income treatment
Whether treaty provisions were incorporated into domestic law by section 788(3)
Whether ACT payments breached Article 56 and whether Article 57(1) applied
Availability of Woolwich or Kleinwort Benson restitution remedies

enrichment.short_title: Representation agreement for Guinean lease-management deal enforceable despite intermediaries' prior government relationships
key_facts: Tekron, controlled by Karjian, Safwat and Nounou, negotiated the 1999 lease-management agreement for Friguia alumina refinery in Guinea on behalf of Reynolds and Guinea Investment Company (GIC).
GIC agreed to pay Tekron a $4m initial fee plus carrying fees over 25 years under a representation agreement governed by English law.
After RusAl acquired GIC in December 2002 it refused further payments, alleging the contract was for improper exercise of influence with Guinean officials.
Tekron provided substantial negotiation services; no bribes or corrupt payments were alleged; Guinean investigation found no impropriety.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court trial of claim for carrying fees and counterclaim for repayment of fees already paid; defence of illegality under Guinean Article 195 and English public policy.
enrichment.outcome: Claim succeeded; representation agreement enforceable; counterclaim dismissed.
enrichment.ratio: Article 195 of the Guinean Criminal Code targets abuse of influence (trafic d'influence), not legitimate commercial representation where genuine services are performed without intending to procure decisions contrary to the public authority's interests; English public policy does not bar payment for intermediaries who use established professional relationships to negotiate complex transactions, as distinguished from sale of influence in Montefiore and Lemenda.
legal_issues: Whether the agreement was a contract to sell improper influence with Guinean government officials
Whether performance was illegal under Guinean Article 195
Whether the agreement offended English public policy
Construction of Tekron's duties under clauses 2 and 4 of the representation agreement
